finding: THE CLEANEST PROOF OF CONCEPT. Urinary clearance of the Oatp1a1 substrate E2-17betaG was >250-FOLD LOWER in male than female rats, with NO comparable sex difference in biliary excretion or renal metabolism, and with plasma protein binding and inulin clearance EQUAL between sexes (excluding GFR and binding). A >250-fold, androgen-reversible, reabsorption-driven renal clearance sex difference is therefore achievable in the rat through Oatp1a1 alone - comfortably larger than the 20-70x PFOA sex difference that needs explaining

measurement: urinary and fecal [14C]PFOA elimination (9.4 pmol/kg IV on GD16) and renal transporter expression after testosterone propionate s/c GD15-20 (2-fold rise in plasma testosterone)
hormone_regulation: TESTOSTERONE, administered to the INTACT (pregnant) FEMALE rat
evidence_type: in vivo hormone administration + 14C mass balance + renal transporter expression
finding: Doubling plasma testosterone in pregnant rats REDUCED total PFOA elimination (urine plus feces) by 12% and raised tissue PFOA concentrations by 12%. Renal Oat2 and Oat3 expression significantly DECREASED while Oatp1 and Oat-K expression significantly INCREASED - exactly the direction predicted by the Kudo 2002 / Lu 1996 model. Fecal excretion was minimal and unchanged; PFOA distribution was highest in placenta, then kidney, liver, brain, heart, lung, spleen. NOTE THE SMALL EFFECT SIZE (12%) for a 2-fold acute testosterone rise, far short of the 20-70x sex difference - the full male phenotype evidently requires chronic, pubertal-onset androgen exposure rather than an acute 2-fold increase

measurement: % of a single 50 mg/kg IP dose excreted in urine in 24 h
hormone_regulation: OESTRADIOL STIMULATES excretion; castration partially mimics it
evidence_type: castration + oestradiol replacement in male rats
finding: Intact FEMALES excreted 72 +/- 5% (n=6) of the dose in urine in 24 h vs only 9 +/- 4% (n=6) in intact MALES - an 8-fold difference. Castration followed by oestradiol (500 ug/kg every 2nd day for 14 days) raised male excretion to 68 +/- 14% (n=10), i.e. the female level; oestradiol alone in non-castrated males gave 61 +/- 19% (n=10); castration alone significantly enhanced renal PFOA excretion but less effectively than oestradiol. At 96 h serum PFOA in intact males was 17-40x higher than in all other groups. PFOA was bound similarly by male and female serum proteins, and no phase II metabolism was detected in either sex

measurement: urinary [1-14C]PFOA elimination (9.4 umol/kg IP) after castration, castration + 17beta-estradiol, castration + physiological testosterone, ovariectomy, ovariectomy + testosterone, and probenecid
hormone_regulation: TESTOSTERONE INHIBITS renal PFOA excretion; a MALE-SPECIFIC response
finding: Whole-body t1/2 male 15 d vs female <1 d. CASTRATION greatly increased urinary PFOA elimination, proving a testicular factor causes slow male elimination. Castration + 17beta-estradiol had NO FURTHER effect beyond castration alone; castration + physiological testosterone replacement returned elimination to the intact-male level. In FEMALES, NEITHER ovariectomy NOR ovariectomy + testosterone affected urinary PFOA elimination, so the testosterone effect is a MALE-SPECIFIC response. PROBENECID decreased the high renal excretion rate in CASTRATED males but had NO effect in intact males - the probenecid-sensitive secretory pathway is only functionally unmasked when androgen is withdrawn. NOTE: these female results CONFLICT with Kudo 2002, which reported that ovariectomy significantly INCREASED and testosterone significantly DECREASED PFOA CL_R in female rats

finding: Biliary PFOA was LOWER in Abcb4-null mice (0.25 +/- 0.12 ug/mL) than wild-type (0.87 +/- 0.02 ug/mL), and ABCB4 was localised immunohistochemically to the apical region of hepatocytes - ABCB4 is a BILIARY efflux transporter for PFOA in the mouse. Renal clearance of PFOA was HIGHER in Abcb4-null mice (compensation): of 642 transporters, 5 differed, including Abcb1 and Slc22a8 (Oat3); renal Abcb1 mRNA was higher and Abcb1b protein enhanced in proximal tubules, while Slc22a8 was not. In Abcb1a/b-null mice renal PFOA clearance was significantly DECREASED. Conclusion: Abcb4 and Abcb1 are excretory transporters of PFOA into bile and urine respectively. The paper notes PFOA plasma t1/2 is 15-20 d in mice, <1-15 d in rats and 20-35 d in cynomolgus monkeys, and that the long human half-life reflects 'the virtual absence of renal excretion' in humans, with biliary excretion high relative to renal

measurement: systematic compilation of every study that directly assessed PFAS uptake by renal transporters (Table 2), plus a sex/species-difference annotation per transporter (Table 1)
finding: Table 1 annotates SLCO1A1 (rat Oatp1a1/Oatp1) with 'Y/Y' for BOTH a sex difference AND a human-rat species difference, and SLC22A7 (Oat2) with 'Y/N'. Human OAT4 and URAT1 (apical uptake) and rat Oatp1a1 (apical uptake) are the identified REABSORPTIVE transporters for PFOA; human OAT1/OAT3 and rat Oat1/Oat3 (basolateral uptake) are the SECRETORY ones; human OATP2B1 and ASBT take PFOS up from urine with a potency order PFOS>PFHxS>PFNA>PFOA>PFBS for OATP2B1. Transporter-facilitated uptake dominates: passive diffusion contributes only 5-60% of total cellular PFAS uptake. Table 2 lists the 9 primary in vitro studies: Nakagawa 2008 (OAT1/2/3, PFOA), Nakagawa 2009 (OAT4, PFOA), Zhao 2015 (ASBT, PFBS/PFHxS/PFOS), Yang 2010 (OATP1A2/OAT4/URAT1, C4-C12 PFCAs), Zhao 2017 (OATPs, PFBS/PFHxS/PFOS), Weaver 2010 (Oat1/2/3, Oatp1a1, Urat1, C2-C18 PFCAs), Katakura 2007 (Oatp1, Oat3, Npt2, Mrp2, PFOA), Yang 2009 (Oatp1a1, PFOA), Louisse 2023 (OAT4, C7-C10 PFCAs plus PFBS/PFHxS/PFOS). The review also notes that probenecid could inhibit PFOA reabsorption in humans (via URAT1) but not in the rat, and that URAT1 'could also be responsible for species differences in PFOA elimination'. For sex differences in HUMANS it states that 'to the best of our knowledge, no human renal transporters to date have been specifically identified as responsible', and that human sex differences may be largely non-renal (menstruation, breast-feeding, transplacental transfer)

finding: 'the primary difference between male and female clearance occurred in the RAT... this sex-dependent difference is NOT consistently observed across mice and non-human primates, indicating that there may be something unique about male vs. female rats such as a sex hormone-dependence on kidney transporters.' The paper cites male rat castration reducing Oat3 in the renal cortex (Ljubojevic 2004) and reducing Oatp1a1 in MOUSE (Cheng 2006) and RAT (Gotoh 2002) kidney, with restoration by testosterone in each species - i.e. Zurlinden et al. themselves note that the mouse transporter IS androgen-regulated. They also find that IV routes generally produced LARGER clearances than gavage in the rat, significantly so for female rats for PFBA, PFBS, PFHxS, PFOA, PFOS and PFDA (apparent bioavailability >100%), which violates classical PK assumptions. MOUSE DATA COVERAGE IS THIN: mouse fits rest on Chang 2012 (PFOS), Chang 2008 (PFBA), Daikin 2010 (PFHxA), Gannon 2011 (PFHxA), Lau 2020 (PFBS), Lou 2009 (PFOA), Sundstrom 2012 (PFHxS) and Tatum-Gibbs 2011 (PFNA) - for PFOA, PFHxS and PFNA in the mouse there is only ONE source study each, so the large mouse/rat half-life ratios for those three chemicals rest on a single mouse experiment apiece

hormone_regulation: androgen-dependent, MALE-predominant
finding: Rat Oat1 and Oat3 are expressed in a male-dominant manner in kidney; male rat castration significantly REDUCES Oat3 expression in the renal cortex and testosterone restores it. NOTE THE DIRECTIONAL PROBLEM: Oat1/Oat3 are SECRETORY, so male-predominant Oat1/Oat3 would make male rats eliminate PFOA FASTER, the opposite of what is observed. This is precisely why the field converged on apical Oatp1a1 reabsorption rather than basolateral secretion as the explanation, and it means the Kudo 2002 regression on Oat2/Oat3 is directionally awkward. finding: HEPATIC concentrations of PFNA, PFOA and PFHpA were HIGHER IN MALE than in female MICE; PFHpA accumulated less and PFHxA barely at all. So the MOUSE DOES HAVE A SEX DIFFERENCE in hepatic PFCA accumulation even where the serum half-life difference is small. There was NO significant sex-related difference in the induction of peroxisomal beta-oxidation by any PFCA, and a single regression line related beta-oxidation activity to hepatic PFCA concentration across C6-C9 in male mice - the potency ordering PFNA>PFOA>PFHpA>PFHxA is explained by hepatic concentration, not intrinsic potency. PFHpA and PFOA did NOT induce peroxisomal beta-oxidation in FEMALE rat liver whereas PFNA and PFDA did - a direct toxicodynamic consequence of the toxicokinetic sex difference. Chain-length potency differences are fully explained by hepatic concentration ('the difference in their chemical structure is not the cause of the difference in the potency of the induction')
